text: A romance that keeps restarting is hard to film, since the part worth watching is never the reunion but the stretch of years in between. Jorge writes for a left-leaning magazine in Buenos Aires while the military government decides what a magazine may print; Laura acts. They meet, they separate, he goes on being afraid of the word commitment, and his fortunes thin out. Twenty years pass this way and the country changes around them, which is the sly arrangement here: a couple who can settle nothing measured against a nation settling something in public. Campanella works in comedy, which costs him no seriousness and buys him patience. The Silver Condor went to both leads, and the arithmetic is plain enough — this is a picture that lives on two faces aging at their own rate.

The gates of a mountain fortress close in December, and the war that follows is conducted largely in sentences. The fortress of Namhan, winter of 1636: the Qing have crossed into Joseon, and King In-jo, loyal to a Ming court that is already losing China, has refused to bow to the Khan who now calls himself emperor. What a siege does to the people shut inside it is force them to keep talking — about the cold, about supply, about which humiliation can be survived — while the cavalry outside waits. Hwang Dong-hyuk takes 140 minutes over that, and the length is the argument: a decision made slowly by men who understand their names will stay attached to it. It won an audience award at IFFR, so the debate evidently carries for viewers who arrive without the seventeenth century in hand.

An aging actor brings his troupe into a small town where he once left a woman, and the bookings are not the reason he came. The son is his. Years of touring have kept that at a workable distance, and the visit ends the distance. Ozu holds 86 minutes at the level of rooms, meals and idle hours between performances, with a man doing arithmetic on the life he took instead of this one, while the mistress he arrived with reads the situation faster than anyone means her to. Kinema Junpo voted it the best Japanese film of 1934. The cruelty gets distributed rather than assigned: nobody here is only wronged, and nobody is only at fault, including the woman with the most reason to be furious. Small company, small town, and no room in either for a private arrangement to stay private.

The news comes secondhand, from a boy in the neighborhood: Tekla has been seen crossing into Turkey. Lia, retired from teaching, has had no contact with her transgender niece in years, and she goes anyway — the kind of errand people take on when the alternative is sitting still. Achi comes along, unpredictable, not much comfort, indispensable because he is the one who knows anything. Istanbul absorbs them both. Levan Akin shoots in Georgian out of Denmark, and the film keeps the pace of two people with no plan putting questions to strangers in a city that owes them nothing. He took the Guldbagge for direction, and what the award is paying for shows in how seldom the camera stops to explain a person. The search stays an errand rather than a lesson.

Two things happen to João at once: he falls for a girl who plays punk records, and he takes work in a trade that already has an owner. What follows comes out of the overlap. He had arrived looking for a better life, the least exotic motive available and the one that has put more people in front of dangerous men than any other. René Sampaio has 108 minutes to carry an arrival, a love affair and a drug lord with a long memory, so events land faster than the people inside them can think, and the compression is the texture. Maria comes with her own noise instead of serving as scenery for a man's decline. The Grande Prêmio do Cinema Brasileiro named it the year's best film; on the evidence of the setup, what got rewarded is a crime picture willing to spend its first stretch on happiness.

Physiognomy was a paying trade, and its best clients were people making appointments and enemies at the same time. The man at the center of this can look at a face and say what its owner will do, a skill worth a fortune at court and worth nothing at all once the court begins using it. A child holds the throne; his uncle intends to take it; both sides would like a reading, and a reading in that room is not a description but an act. Han Jae-rim spends 140 minutes on the machinery of a palace coup, where the live question is not who prevails but what a specialist owes the people who consult him. It holds the Grand Bell for best film. There is a fine joke buried in the premise: if faces are destiny, the one face the reader cannot get in front of is his own.

Two sisters in the Gion agree on every fact of their situation and draw opposite conclusions from it. The elder has taken in a man who turned up bankrupt after leaving his wife; she feels an obligation, and in Kyoto in 1936 an obligation of that kind comes with a price attached. The younger has done the sums: sentiment is the one thing women in their line cannot afford, and a patron with money is a working arrangement rather than a betrayal. Mizoguchi lets both of them be right, which is harder to sit with than letting either be wrong. Sixty-nine minutes, and the film moves like something with a train to catch. The house is shown as a place of work, with hours and clients and rent, and the rent does not care which sister turns out to have been correct.

Sugihara was born in Japan, as was the generation before him, and the country still files him under elsewhere. That the film is also a romance is the decision that makes it work: the weight lands in the small transactions of being seventeen — introductions, questions about where he comes from, the arithmetic of what to say and to whom — rather than in speeches. Two hours is enough time for the question to get asked of him more than once, in different tones, by people who each think they are asking it for the first time. Isao Yukisada stays with the boy well past the point where a shorter film would have made its case and gone home. Japan submitted it to the Academy Awards that year, which carries its own irony: a country putting forward a picture about someone it declines to count as one of its own.

In Paris, a company of exiled Argentinians has a tango-ballet to stage, and exile turns out to be a rehearsal problem. The piece is dedicated to Carlos Gardel, and the obstacles are the ordinary ones of any production — money, tempers, a form that resists the stage — with the difference that nobody in the room chose the city they are working in. Solanas made it as a musical, and the choice commits him: across 119 minutes the numbers have to carry what the characters will not say plainly, and neither the music nor the argument can be allowed to slacken. Venice gave it the Grand Jury Prize. The parts likeliest to stay with a viewer are the rehearsals rather than any finished number, people assembling something elaborate and Argentine in a place that did not ask for it, on the reasoning that stopping would be worse.

The swindle is a correspondence school of journalism: no school, no faculty, only lessons mailed to people who would like to write for a living. The man running it failed at exactly that, which is what makes the pitch good — he knows what the mark is hoping for, having hoped it. His partner is a Hungarian immigrant with no stake in Buenos Aires beyond what the scheme returns. It holds the Silver Condor for best film, and it is built as a thriller in which nobody is being chased: 92 minutes, tuition envelopes arriving from strangers, an arrangement that works precisely as long as neither man looks straight at it. The pressure comes from inside the partnership. That is harder to stage than a pursuit, and cheaper, and it does not go out of date.

Three women with high school diplomas enroll in the company English course, because the promotion they want has a rung they are not permitted to skip. Mid-1990s Korea, a large firm, three desks positioned low enough that nobody upstairs wonders what crosses them. Then something in the paperwork stops adding up. Lee Jong-pil keeps the comedy in the friendship and the trouble in the documents and never has to separate the two: stubbornness, patience and the habit of checking are what make the three funny together and what make them a problem for their employer. Corruption, in this telling, is a filing matter. The mid-nineties setting is not nostalgia either — it is close to the last moment when a company's secrets lived on paper that somebody had to carry down a hallway.

Eighty-seven minutes, three men, one drug dealer to be removed, and no time budgeted for anybody's reasons. The team is assembled from incompatible parts: Ryuichi Koga fights as a ninja, Takeshi Hayato worked narcotics as a detective before he began killing for money, and Ichiro Sakura contributes arrangement rather than violence. A picture this lean holds together on tempo rather than plot, with room for roughly one idea per reel, and the idea had better move. The pleasures Teruo Ishii is working with in 1974 are craft pleasures: staging, timing, the order in which men come through a door. It is a genre exercise without an alibi. Any account that reaches after larger meanings is padding the one thing whose whole virtue is that it refuses to be padded.

Summer in Hakodate is short, and the film allows itself exactly that long. He has thrown love away; she has given up on it. From outside the two conditions look identical and inside they are nothing alike, one being a decision and the other an accumulation, and the difference is the film's entire occupation. Mipo O takes 120 minutes over a few weeks in a northern port, generous for a story with this little incident in it, and the generosity is the method: reasons of that kind surface at their own speed or not at all. Kinema Junpo named it the best Japanese film of its year. What the setting supplies is limit rather than atmosphere — a season with an end date, a town where the same people keep turning up, two adults who have each settled in advance how much they are prepared to want.

The beluga hunt off the Ile-aux-Coudres stopped in 1924, and in 1963 it was a film crew, not a market, that asked whether it could be done again. The documentary is therefore the cause of what it documents, and Perrault puts that on the record instead of hiding it. The young men take the work on as something owed to the dead: the method has to be reassembled out of what older islanders can still describe, on a stretch of the St. Lawrence where the tide sets the working hours. 106 minutes of preparation, talk and waiting on water, and the talk is the substance, since reviving a practice means first agreeing on what it was. It carries a Canadian Screen Award for best motion picture, a strange honor for a film whose subject existed because someone pointed a camera at it.
